Dear Ms. Brennan,

Thank you for your note and for the materials, which I read over the weekend with real interest. Your honors work on astrocyte calcium signalling in Professor Achterberg's group is closer to what we do than most of the applications I see. We have spent the better part of two years trying to work out whether the slow calcium waves we record in hippocampal slices are doing anything at all, or are merely, as one reviewer rather unkindly put it, "the tissue sighing." The position we have open for the coming year would sit squarely inside that question: a good deal of two-photon imaging, some slice work once you are trained, and rather more analysis in Python than most applicants expect.

I would be very glad to speak with you about it. I should confess, however, that my calendar is in a state I can only describe as geological, and I long ago stopped pretending to manage it myself. I am therefore copying Beatrix Olander, our lab manager, who keeps my schedule and who in any case knows the day-to-day of the position better than I do. She will be in touch with a few options for a conversation of perhaps forty-five minutes, and may also arrange for you to meet one or two of the current RAs while you are here.

With best wishes,

Corwin Strathmore, PhD
Associate Professor of Neurobiology

Jalen,

I've read through the draft of your regression project. The mixed-effects specification is a sensible choice given that you have repeated race times per swimmer, but I'd like you to justify the random slope on meet altitude. With only six meets, I suspect it isn't well identified. Try a likelihood-ratio test against the random-intercept-only model and report both.

On the data side: the splits from the two meets where electronic timing failed should be flagged rather than imputed. Your current imputation pulls them toward the swimmer means, which is exactly the kind of shrinkage you're trying to estimate. A sensitivity analysis with and without those meets would be stronger.

Also, the department is collecting abstracts for the spring undergraduate research showcase. Your project would be a good fit; the deadline is January 15, and I'm happy to read a draft abstract over break.

One logistical thing: I'll be at a conference next week, so I need to move our Tuesday 4:00 appointment. Could we do Monday, November 30 at 2:00 PM instead, same place?

Otherwise, nice work. The residual diagnostics section is the clearest I've seen from an undergraduate this term.
